results.content:
Title: What do we mean by effective sample size? | Statistical Odds & Ends
# What do we mean by effective sample size? A typical estimation strategy is to draw independent and identically distributed samples from F (i.e. X_1, \dots, X_n \stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} F), then plug those samples into an estimator T_n = T(X_1, \dots, X_n). The sample size is the number of samples we have: n. ***But what happens if our samples are not i.i.d.?*** In an extreme example, imagine that we have samples X_1, \dots, X_n, but our sampling design forced the restriction X_1 = \dots = X_n. While it looks like we have n numbers, intuitive we know we really only have one sample. ***Effective sample size*** makes this idea concrete. When X_1, \dots, X_n are i.i.d. from F, the estimator has a certain variance \text{Var}(T_n). If our samples come from some other sampling design, we will have a different expression for the variance. Effective sample size is the number n_{eff} such that when we compute the estimator based on n samples from our sampling design, the resulting variance is \text{Var}(T_{n_{eff}}). While different estimators could give rise to different effective sample sizes, estimation of the mean via the sample mean is so common that when someone talks about effective sample size, it is almost always with respect to this estimator. If our X_i‘s are not drawn from the i.i.d. sampling design, then the effective sample size is n_{eff} such that. The notion of effective sample size comes up frequently in two contexts: when observations are correlated (e.g. time series data or Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation) or weighted. Hence, we need expressions for the covariance to compute effective sample size. In this setting, the observations are i.i.d. but each observation X_i is given an observation weight w_i \geq 0. These weights should affect our sample size. Taking an extreme example, if w_1 = 1 and w_2 = \dots = w_n = 0, our estimator is really using only X_1 and not the other samples, so the effective sample size should be 1. * Share on X (Opens in new window) X. ## 1 thought on “What do we mean by effective sample size?”. 1. With the exception of unweighted sample size, all statistics computed by Q take into account the weight. Q uses two methods to compute effective sample size. Where Taylor series linearization is not used, Kish's Effective Sample Size Formula is used. * Where a data file has been weighted, most tables in Q report the *effective sample size* in the bottom-right corner of the screen. The effective sample size at the bottom of a table is computed as follows:. * In some statistical tests the effective sample size is used to modify the weight (see Weight Calibration). However, from Q4.10 onwards, Q also permits an additional design effect (**Extra deff** in **Statistical Assumptions**) to be taken into account in significance testing to reflect aspects of the sample design that are not taken into account by the weight. The un-weighted sample size divided by the supplied extra design effect is used in all statistical inference.

results.title: Weights, Effective Sample Size, and Design Effects – Technical Documentation
results.content: # Weights, Effective Sample Size, and Design Effects. With the exception of unweighted sample size, all statistics computed take into account the weight. ## Effective sample size. The effective sample size is a measure of the precision of the survey (e.g., even if you have a sample of 1,000 people, an effective sample size of 100 would indicate that the weighted sample is no more robust than a well-executed un-weighted simple random sample of 100 people). Q and Displayr use two methods to compute effective sample size. Where Taylor series linearization is not used, Kish's Effective Sample Size Formula is used. Note that the design effect, discussed in the next section, also impacts the effective sample size. Q and Displayr also permit an additional design effect (**Extra deff** in **Statistical Assumptions**) to be taken into account in significance testing to reflect aspects of the sample design that are not taken into account by the weight.

results.content:
Title: r - Reduced effective sample size in balanced population after inverse probability treatment weighting - Cross Validated
# Reduced effective sample size in balanced population after inverse probability treatment weighting. Weighting involves estimating a weight for each unit in the sample and then estimating the treatment effect in a way that incorproates the weights, such as weighted linear regression, weighted maximum likelihood, or a weighted difference (or ratio, etc.) in means. Similarly, having a unit with a weight of 2 is not the same as having 2 units; choosing to use one unit's information twice doesn't give you more information about your sample; you are just changing the importance of a unit's contribution to your estimates. The ratio of the variance (i.e., square of the standard error) of the estimate of a mean from a weighted sample to the estimate of a mean from an unweighted sample is known as the "design effect" (i.e., the effect of the "design" on the precision of the estimate) and was derived by Shook-Sa and Hudgens (2020) to be. where $N$ is the sample size of the group and $w\_i$ is the weight for unit $i$. and represents the size of an unweighted sample that contains the same precision as a weighted sample. That is, if you have a sample of 1000 units but after weighting the sample has an ESS of 500, then you will have (approximately) the same precision as if you only had 500 units in an unweighed sample. The fact that weighting retains all units doesn't mean the estimates will be as precise as had you not done weighting at all; in fact, the ESS from IPTW can be smaller than the remaining sample size after matching. The frequencies are the same as they prior to weighting; you will still have the same number of events, the same number of patients with conditions, etc., but those patients will contribute different amounts of information to the estimation of the effect and change the precision accordingly. It is useful, though, to think about weighted means and proportions of variables, since these represent balance in the weighted sample. It means the weighted sample is meant to represent a population in which 40% are married.
